questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Splitting the kinetic energy of a rolling solid cylinder
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the energy of a rolling solid cylinder splits
questions.stem: A practice problem sheet compares the translation and rotation of a rolling solid cylinder; how does its kinetic energy split? Explain.

answer.exemplar: For a rolling solid cylinder the centre of mass moves at speed v and the body turns at angular speed omega, with omega equal to v over the radius. The translational part of the kinetic energy is half m v squared and the rotational part is half I omega squared, and with I equal to half m R squared the second term becomes one quarter of m v squared. The total is therefore three quarters of m v squared, split one third to translation and two thirds to rotation.

questions.explanation: For a rolling solid cylinder the translational energy is half m v squared and the rotational part adds one quarter of that, so the total is three quarters of m v squared. The rotation carries two thirds of the energy.
questions.hint: Rolling without slipping links omega to v over the radius.

questions.stem: A study group sheet evaluates why a hoop is harder to spin up than a disk of the same size and mass; explain the reasoning.

questions.topic: Angular impulse delivered to a rotating body
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an angular impulse is and how it changes a body
questions.stem: A practice problem sheet compares what an angular impulse is and how it changes a spinning body; explain the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: An angular impulse is a torque applied over a time, and by the rotational impulse-momentum relation it produces a change in angular momentum equal to the impulse. For a body whose inertia does not change, the change in angular speed is the impulse divided by the moment of inertia, so a given impulse slows a wheel with a large inertia less than it slows a light one. The impulse can also add energy or take it away, depending on which way it is applied.

questions.explanation: An angular impulse changes the angular momentum, so for a fixed inertia the angular speed changes by the impulse over the inertia. The same impulse therefore affects a large inertia less than a small one.
questions.hint: An impulse acts on the angular momentum of the body.

questions.explanation: A uniform solid sphere about a diameter has the value two fifths of m R squared, 0.4 x 2.5 x 0.16 = 0.16 kg m^2. The same mass and radius as a thin shell would give two thirds of m R squared.
questions.hint: A solid sphere about a diameter uses two fifths.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Angular acceleration of a rod from a net torque
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the net torque needed for a stated angular acceleration
questions.stem: The revision hand-outs track the net torque that gives a hoop of inertia 0.80 kg m^2 an angular acceleration of 2.5 rad/s^2, in newton metres.
questions.explanation: The torque required is I alpha, so 0.80 x 2.5 = 2.0 N m. Because the hoop carries more inertia than a disk of the same size, it needs more torque for the same angular acceleration.
questions.hint: Torque equals inertia times angular acceleration.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Angular speed and angle turned under constant angular acceleration
questions.learningObjective: Find the final speed and angle of a wheel already turning
questions.stem: A group study task asks about a wheel already turning at 8 rad/s that accelerates at 2 rad/s^2 for 5 s; first find the final speed, then the angle turned.

options.text: The final speed is 18 rad/s and the angle is 25 rad, ignoring the starting speed.
options.misconception: ignores the starting speed in the angle turned

options.text: The final speed is 10 rad/s and the angle is 65 rad, adding the speeds wrongly.
options.misconception: adds the starting and final speeds for the change

options.text: The final speed is 18 rad/s and the angle is 65 rad, since the starting speed keeps turning.
The final speed is 18 rad/s and the angle is 40 rad, counting only the initial speed.
options.misconception: counts only the initial speed in the angle turned

questions.explanation: The final speed is omega zero plus alpha t, 8 + 10 = 18 rad/s, and the angle is omega zero t plus half alpha t squared, 40 + 25 = 65 rad. The starting speed keeps contributing to the angle.
questions.hint: Include the starting speed in both results.
